section_1.title: The Intuitive Hook: The Prism Analogy
section_1.content: Introduce the concept of decomposition. Just as a prism splits white light into a rainbow of colors, the Fourier Transform splits a complex signal into its fundamental sine and cosine frequencies.
section_1.example: Visualizing a 'smoothie' vs. its ingredients: If a signal is a smoothie, the Fourier Transform identifies the exact amounts of strawberry, banana, and yogurt used to make it.

section_2.title: Prerequisite Review: Periodic Oscillations
section_2.content: Briefly revisit the components of a wave: Amplitude (height), Frequency (cycles per second), and Phase (shift). Use a graphical animation showing multiple sine waves layering to form a complex 'jagged' wave.
section_2.example: Visualizing a clock hand rotating: As it spins faster, the frequency increases, forming the basis of a circular motion that represents our sine waves.

section_3.title: The Core Concept: Moving from Time to Frequency
section_3.content: Explain the transition from the Time Domain (where we see events happening over time) to the Frequency Domain (where we see the 'DNA' of the signal). Focus on the integral formula as a process of matching the signal against a 'reference frequency'.
section_3.example: An audio recording of a bird chirping: In the time domain, it's a messy waveform; in the frequency domain, it becomes a distinct spike at the frequency of the chirp.

section_4.title: The Fourier Transform Integral: Decoding the Signature
section_4.content: Explain the concept of correlation: the transform 'multiplies' the signal by a pure sine wave and integrates. If they match, the result is high; if they don't, it cancels out. This 'sifts' out the hidden frequencies.
section_4.example: A 'Lock and Key' animation: Imagine the Fourier transform as a set of master keys (sine waves of different sizes). Only the key that matches the frequency 'unlocks' the signal's energy at that spot.

section_5.title: Application: The Digital World
section_5.content: Show how the Fourier Transform is the engine behind modern technology. By identifying frequencies, we can compress data by removing frequencies humans can't hear or see.
section_5.example: MP3 compression: The Fourier Transform identifies high-frequency sounds the human ear can't hear, allowing us to 'discard' them to make the file size smaller without affecting perceived audio quality.
